d: What React is, the mental model it asks you to adopt, and where React 19 fits today.
h: Why re-rendering is not a performance problem
b: Overview React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components. It gives you a way to describe what the screen should look like for a given set of data, and it takes responsibility for making the real DOM match that description. React is deliberately not a framework. It ships a component model, a rendering engine, and a set of hooks. It does not ship a router, a data layer, a build tool, or an opinion about your folder structure. You either assemble those yourself or adopt a framework built on React that has already chosen them for you. That narrowness is the trade. You get flexibility and a very large ecosystem; you also get a list of decisions to make before you write your first feature. The rest of this site is largely about making those decisions well. Where React 19 sits today React 19.0 was the large release: it introduced Actions, the use() API, Server Components as a stable feature, and it removed a decade of accumulated legacy API. d: The syntax React uses to describe UI, and what the compiler turns it into.
h: One root element, or a Fragment
Attributes are props, and they are camelCase
Curly braces open a JavaScript expression
What renders and what does not
Passing an element as a prop
b: Overview JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript. It looks like HTML, but it is compiled away before it ever reaches the browser. Every JSX tag becomes a plain function call that returns a plain object describing what you want on screen. That object is a React element. It is a description, not a DOM node. React reads the description and decides what to do with the real DOM. Because JSX is JavaScript, everything you already know applies: variables, function calls, map, ternaries, template literals. There is no separate template language to learn and no separate set of control-flow keywords. Why it exists Rendering logic and markup are not separable in practice. The condition that decides whether a button is disabled lives next to the button. JSX lets you keep them in the same file, in the same expression, without inventing a template dialect. The alternative is writing element calls by hand: That is legal and still works, but it becomes unreadable three levels deep. When not to use it You can skip JSX entirely if you cannot add a build step. React ships createElement for exactly that case, and libraries such as htm offer a tagged-template alternative. Both are niche. Every mainstream React toolchain compiles JSX for you, so the default answer is to use it. Do not use JSX to build strings. If you need HTML as text, produce the string directly. JSX produces objects, not markup. B

d: The function that takes props and returns UI, and the purity rule that makes it work.
h: Purity: the rule that everything else depends on
b: Overview A component is a JavaScript function that takes an object of props and returns what should appear on screen. That is the entire contract. Two conventions turn a function into a component: its name starts with a capital letter, and it returns React elements (or null). Nothing else is required — no base class, no registration, no decorator. Components compose. A page is a component that renders layout components, which render feature components, which render form controls. The same mechanism works at every level, which is why React has no concept of "widget" versus "page". Why it exists Splitting a UI into components buys three things. Reuse. A <Button> written once looks the same everywhere and changes in one place. Isolation. State declared inside a component belongs to that component instance. Two <SearchBox /> elements have independent state without any extra work. A rendering boundary. React tracks components individually, so when state changes it re-renders that component's subtree rather than the whole app. The boundaries you draw are the boundaries React optimizes along. When to use it Extract a component when a piece of markup has its own name, its own state, or its own reason to change. d: How data flows into a component, why it is read-only, and what changed in React 19.
b: Overview Props are the arguments you pass to a component. The parent writes them as JSX attributes; the component receives them as one object. Props flow one way: down. A child cannot reach up and change what its parent passed. To let a child affect the parent, the parent passes a function down and the child calls it. Why it exists Props are what make a component reusable. Without them, <PriceTag /> could only ever show one price. The one-way flow is the more important half. When data only moves down, there is exactly one place that owns each value, and you can answer "why did this change?" by walking up the tree. Two-way binding gives you the opposite: any component can write anywhere, and a wrong value has no obvious origin. When to use it Pass a prop when a parent knows something the child needs: data to display, a callback to invoke, an element to render in a slot. Pass a callback prop (onSelect, onDismiss) rather than passing a state setter directly. onSelect={(id) => setSelectedId(id)} keeps the child ignorant of how the parent stores its state, so the parent can switch to a reducer later without touching the child. When not to use it Do not thread a prop through five components that do not use it. d: The memory a component keeps between renders, and why each render sees a frozen snapshot of it.
h: Derived state: compute it, do not store it
b: Overview State is the data a component remembers between renders. A local variable resets every time the function runs; state does not. Two things happen when you call setCount: React stores the new value, and React schedules a re-render of the component. Both matter. State that changed without re-rendering would be invisible; a re-render without stored state would show the old value. This page is about how state behaves. For the full useState API — lazy initializers, the returned setter's identity, resetting with a key — see useState. Why it exists React's model is that the UI is a function of state. You never write "find the button and change its label"; you change the state and describe what the UI looks like for that state. For that to work, React needs a place to keep values that survive a render and that it knows to watch. A module-level variable survives, but React has no way to know it changed. A local variable is watched by nothing and does not survive. State is the one storage that does both. Each component instance gets its own state. Two <Counter /> elements count independently, with no configuration. When to use it Use state for a value that changes over time and affects what is rendered. d: The trigger, render and commit phases, how reconciliation preserves component state, and what concurrent rendering changes.
h: How React decides to keep or recreate a component
Rendering that is not on screen
Reading the phases in the Profiler
Resetting a subtree with a key
b: Overview "Render" in React means one specific thing: React calls your component function and collects the elements it returns. It does not mean "touch the DOM". Those are separate steps, and keeping them separate is what lets React batch, interrupt and prioritize work. Every update goes through three phases: Trigger — something asks for a render: the initial mount, or a state update. Render — React calls the components that need re-rendering and compares the result with the previous one. Commit — React applies the minimum set of DOM changes, then runs layout effects and, after the browser paints, Effects. Why it exists Splitting render from commit is the whole design. Because the render phase only computes objects, React can do it without the user seeing anything. It can throw the work away, redo it, or do it in the background for a route the user has not navigated to yet. Nothing has been shown, so nothing has to be undone. Because the commit phase is a single synchronous pass over a finished result, the user never sees a half-updated screen. There is no moment where the header shows new data and the body shows old data. This is also why your components must be pure. React reserves the right to call them more than once, and to discard the result. When to use it You do not call render. You trigger it, and there are exactly two triggers: The initial render: createRoot(container)

d: Choosing what to render with if, ternaries and logical AND, and what happens to state when a branch disappears.
h: A helper function instead of an inline chain
b: Overview React has no template directives — no v-if, no *ngIf, no {{#if}}. JSX is JavaScript, so you branch with the language: if, the ternary operator, &&, and early returns. Whatever your branch produces gets rendered. null, undefined, true and false render nothing, which is what makes the shorter forms work. Why it exists There is nothing to invent. A component returns a value; conditionals choose the value. The consequence is that everything you know about JavaScript conditions applies, including the type coercion rules that cause the one real trap on this page. The second thing worth understanding is what conditionals do to the tree. Rendering null instead of a component unmounts it: its state is destroyed and its Effects are cleaned up. Conditional rendering is not a visibility switch. When to use it Use conditional rendering when the branches are genuinely different UI, or when the hidden branch should be forgotten: a modal that starts fresh each time, an error message, a route that is not active. When not to use it Do not use it as a way to hide something you want to keep. Tabs that should remember their scroll position and form drafts, a details panel the user toggles constantly, a route you expect them to come back to — those want <Activity mode="hidden">, which preserves state and DOM. Do not use CSS display: none for this either. The DOM stays, but the Effects keep

d: Rendering arrays with map, and why keys are about identity rather than performance.
h: Index keys, and exactly when they break
b: Overview To render a list, turn an array of data into an array of elements. React renders arrays by rendering each item in order. map is the whole API. There is no list component and no loop syntax, because JSX is JavaScript and JavaScript already has map. The interesting part is key. Why it exists A key tells React which item this is across renders. When a list re-renders, React has an old array of elements and a new one. Without keys it can only match them by position: first to first, second to second. That is fine when the list never changes shape, and wrong as soon as items move. With keys, React matches by identity. An item that moved from index 0 to index 3 is recognized as the same item, so its component instance, its state and its DOM node move with it instead of being reused by whatever landed in index 0. The common summary — "keys help React be fast" — is misleading. Keys exist for correctness. The speed is a side effect of not rebuilding the DOM for items that only moved. When to use it Always, when rendering an array. React warns when a key is missing, and the warning is worth fixing rather than silencing. Use a stable identifier that comes from your data: a database id, a slug, a UUID that was generated when the record was created. When not to use it There is no case where a list of elements should have no key. But there are keys you should not use: The array index

Handler props that report meaning, not mechanics
b: Overview You respond to user interaction by passing a function to an event prop: Event props are camelCased (onClick, onChange, onPointerDown), and they take a function, not a string. There is no addEventListener to call and no listener to remove — React attaches and detaches everything as the tree changes. Why it exists Handlers live in JSX for the same reason markup lives in JavaScript: the code that runs on click belongs next to the thing that gets clicked. React also normalizes events. The object your handler receives is a SyntheticEvent — a wrapper with the same interface as the native event (target, currentTarget, preventDefault, stopPropagation) that behaves identically across browsers. The native event is still available on event.nativeEvent when you need it. Under the hood React does not attach a listener to every node. It attaches a small number of listeners to the root container and dispatches from there. Since React 17, those listeners are attached to the root DOM container rather than to document. This is what makes it safe to run two React versions on one page, and it changes how React events interleave with non-React listeners you attach yourself. React 17 also removed event pooling entirely — the event object stays valid after the handler returns, so event.persist() is no longer needed and no longer exists. Effects that must run once per mount
b: Overview <StrictMode> turns on extra checks for the tree inside it. It renders nothing and changes no behavior in production. Every mainstream React starter enables it by default. If your app has it and you are seeing doubled logs, that is Strict Mode working, not a bug. Why it exists React's model assumes your components are pure and your Effects clean up after themselves. Both assumptions are invisible until they are violated, and when they are violated the symptom is usually intermittent: a duplicated network request, a counter that is occasionally off by one, a subscription that leaks only after a route has been visited twice. Strict Mode converts those intermittent bugs into deterministic ones. It does not find new bugs — it makes existing ones happen every time. The stakes rose with React 18 and 19. d: Why hooks must be called at the top level of a component, and what breaks when they are not.
h: Move the condition inside the hook
Extract a component instead of looping
b: Overview Hooks are ordinary JavaScript functions, but React gives them a superpower: they remember things between renders. That memory is bought with two rules. Only call hooks at the top level. Everything else about hooks follows from these two lines. Break them and you do not get a clear crash — you get state that belongs to a different variable. Why it exists React does not know the names of your hooks. When your component renders, React walks a list attached to that component instance and hands out the stored value at each position. React needs a way to attach state to a plain function that has no this, no instance, and no lifetime of its own. Called twice with the same props, it must produce the same output — otherwise React could not re-run it freely, and concurrent rendering would be impossible. But interfaces change over time. useState is the escape hatch: React stores the value outside your function and hands it back on each call, so your function stays pure while the app stays interactive. The setter is not an assignment. It is a request to re-render with a different value. That distinction explains almost every surprise on this page. h: Async work belongs in the handler
Typing a reducer with a discriminated union
b: Overview useReducer moves your state transitions out of event handlers and into one pure function. reducer — (state, action) => nextState. Must be pure. initialArg — the value the initial state is built from. init (optional) — if given, the initial state is init(initialArg) instead of initialArg itself. Returns the current state and a dispatch function. dispatch(action) schedules a re-render whose state is reducer(currentState, action). Why it exists useState scatters update logic across every handler that touches it. In a component with six pieces of state and ten handlers, the rules for how state may change exist only as the sum of those handlers — you cannot read them in one place, and you cannot test them without rendering. A reducer inverts that. Handlers describe what happened ({ type: 'quantity_changed' }); the reducer decides what the state becomes. The result is one function that takes a value and returns a value, which you can unit-test with no React at all. It also removes a class of bugs. Because the reducer receives the current state as an argument, a transition can never read a stale snapshot. When to use it Several values change together. A form with values, errors, touched and isSubmitting has combinations that are invalid; a reducer lets you make them unrepresentable. Cleanup runs more often than you think
Choosing between the three Effect hooks
Before and after: deleting an unnecessary Effect
b: Overview useEffect lets a component synchronize itself with something outside React — a socket, a subscription, a browser API, a chart library, the document title. setup — runs after React commits the render to the DOM. It may return a cleanup function. dependencies (optional) — an array of reactive values. React re-runs the Effect when any of them differs from the previous render, compared with Object.is. [a, b] — run when a or b changes. [] — run only on mount, clean up on unmount. omitted — run after every render. Most Effects people write should not exist. useEffect is an escape hatch out of React, not a lifecycle hook. If the Effect does not talk to a system outside React, there is almost certainly a better tool. That purity is what lets React render your component twice, discard the result, retry at a different priority, or render it on a server. But real applications must touch the outside world. Something has to open the WebSocket, attach the listener and start the observer — and, crucially, something has to undo all of that. useEffect is the seam. d: Measure the DOM and adjust layout before the browser paints.
h: Keeping a message list pinned to the bottom
Measure with an observer, react with useEffect
b: Overview useLayoutEffect has the same signature as useEffect and one difference that defines it: it runs synchronously after React mutates the DOM and before the browser paints. setup — runs after the DOM update, before paint. May return a cleanup function. dependencies (optional) — same rules as useEffect: an array of every reactive value the setup reads, compared with Object.is. Because it runs before paint, a state update made inside it is rendered in the same frame. The user never sees the intermediate position. Because it runs before paint, it also blocks that paint. That is the whole trade. Why it exists Some layout decisions cannot be made until the DOM exists. How tall is this tooltip? Does the menu fit below the button or must it flip above? Where was the scroll position before the new messages arrived? You cannot compute those during render — there is nothing to measure yet. And you cannot compute them in a useEffect, because that runs after paint: the browser would show one frame with the wrong position, then a corrected frame. The user sees a flicker or a jump. useLayoutEffect gives you the one moment where the DOM is real but the screen has not been updated yet: measure, set state, and let React re-render before the pixels reach the screen. d: Read the latest props and state from an Effect without making them dependencies.
h: A callback prop that changes every render
An interval that reads current state

d: Read a value provided higher up the tree without passing it through props.
h: Wrap the context in a custom hook
b: Overview useContext reads the value of the nearest matching provider above the component in the tree. SomeContext — a context created with createContext(defaultValue). Returns the value of the closest <SomeContext> above this component. If there is no provider above it, you get the defaultValue passed to createContext. In React 19 the context object is the provider component: Before React 19 you rendered <ThemeContext.Provider value={...}>. That still works in 19, but it is deprecated: render <ThemeContext> directly instead. A codemod handles the migration — npx codemod@latest react/19/migration-recipe. Why it exists Props flow down one level at a time. When a value is needed by something ten levels deep — the current theme, the signed-in user, the interface language, a router — every component in between has to accept and forward a prop it does not use. That is prop drilling, and it makes intermediate components harder to reuse and harder to change. Context is a way to say "this value is available to everything in this subtree". The provider marks the boundary; any descendant reads it directly, no matter how deep. The trade is explicitness. A component reading context has a dependency you cannot see at its call site. That is why context suits values that are genuinely ambient — and suits ordinary application data much less well. When to use it Themes and appearance: light or d

d: Hold a mutable value that survives re-renders without causing one.
h: Do not read or write ref.current during render
b: Overview useRef gives you a mutable box that React keeps alive across re-renders. It returns the same object on every render, with a single property: Writing to ref.current does not schedule a re-render. That single sentence is the whole hook. Everything else follows from it. There are exactly two things people use it for: DOM refs — pass ref to a JSX element and React writes the DOM node into ref.current after commit, and null on unmount. Instance-like values — a timer id, a WebSocket, a previous value, a "have I already run this" flag. Data the component owns but never renders. Why it exists A function component has no this. Between one render and the next, every local variable is thrown away. State solves that for values you display, but state has a cost: changing it re-renders. Some values must persist without re-rendering. An interval id is the clearest case — nothing on screen depends on it, so re-rendering when it changes would be pure waste, and setting state from the callback that assigns it would loop. useRef is React's escape hatch for exactly that: persistence without reactivity. When to use it You need a DOM node to call an imperative browser API on: focus(), scrollIntoView(), play(), showModal(), getBoundingClientRect(). You need to remember something between renders that no rendered output reads: interval and timeout ids, an AbortController, a third-party library

d: Expose a narrow imperative API on a ref instead of the raw DOM node.
h: Extending the DOM node instead of replacing it
b: Overview useImperativeHandle replaces what a parent gets when it puts a ref on your component. It returns undefined. Without it, ref.current is whatever DOM node you attached ref to. Hand a parent the raw <input> and it can call focus() — but it can also set value, add classes, change disabled, or rip the node out of the document. d: Cache the result of a calculation between re-renders.

d: Mark a state update as non-urgent so React can interrupt it and keep the UI responsive.

d: Show a stale value while a new one renders in the background.

b: Overview useDeferredValue gives you a lagging copy of a value so an expensive subtree can render at a lower priority. d: Subscribe to an external store without tearing under concurrent rendering.
h: A tiny store, written from scratch
b: Overview useSyncExternalStore subscribes a component to a data source that lives outside React. It returns the current snapshot. When the store notifies, React re-renders the subscribed components. Why it exists Before React 18, the way to read an external mutable source was an Effect: read the value, setState, subscribe, clean up. That worked because rendering was synchronous — nothing could change between the start and end of a render pass. Concurrent rendering broke that assumption. React can now render a tree in interruptible chunks, and the store can be mutated in the middle. d: Label a custom hook in React DevTools.

h: Controlled and uncontrolled, at component scale

You then write synchronization code (usually an Effect) to keep them equal, and that code is a bug factory. Lifting removes the second copy instead of synchronizing it. d: Pass a value to an entire subtree without threading it through every component in between.
h: The default value, and the bug it hides
Two escapes from the re-render problem
Compose providers by nesting, not by merging
Scope a context to a component family

d: Combine useReducer with a state context and a dispatch context to share complex state across a subtree.

b: Overview "Caching" covers three unrelated layers that people routinely conflate: React ships an API for the first, deliberately ships nothing for the second, and has nothing to do with the third. Most "why is this refetching" questions are about the layer the asker was not thinking about. Why it exists On the server, a single render tree may ask for the same record from five different components. Without memoization that is five database round trips for one page, and no component is in a position to know that another one already asked. cache() solves exactly that, and nothing more. It is a per-request memoization table, not a data store. It exists because request-scoped deduplication is the one caching problem that React can solve without inventing a policy — the lifetime is unambiguous, because the request ends. b: Overview Next.js has a family of functions that stop rendering and hand control to the framework. Wiring it into a Next.js build by hand would mean a Babel config, which changes how Turbopack compiles every file you own. d: What Link prefetches by default, what prefetch={true} costs in server work, and how 16.x reduces prefetch requests and bytes.
b: Overview Prefetching makes navigations fast by downloading a route's JavaScript, CSS and RSC payload before the click. It is not free. Every prefetch is a request, and a prefetch that renders dynamic content is server work for a page the user may never open. In production, <Link> prefetches when it enters the viewport. How much it fetches depends on the route and on the prefetch prop: Prefetching is disabled in development, so next dev never shows you its cost. Why it exists Server Components move rendering to the server, so a click on an un-prefetched link waits on a network round trip before anything changes. Prefetching pays that cost ahead of time. The trade-off is that you pay it for every visible link, not for every clicked link. A page with 200 product cards pays for 200 prefetches. Next.js 16.0 and 16.3 shipped changes that make the default cheaper, so the question for most apps is no longer whether to prefetch but where to stop the defaults from over-fetching. When to use it Read this page when: Server logs or bills show far more RSC requests than page views. A page with long lists of links (feeds, tables, search results) generates a burst of requests on scroll. You are about to add prefetch={true} to make a navigation feel instant. Layouts or pages run side effects, such as analytics, that should only run on a real visit. When not to use it Do not turn prefetching off
